scenes.title: Safety begins before anything goes wrong
scenes.lead: A sample is only useful if collecting it does not injure someone. Preventive safety means noticing and controlling hazards before work. Emergency response means acting in an organized way if something still goes wrong. This step develops prevention and preparation; the next two steps teach responses to injuries, heat illness, spills and evacuation.
scenes.narration:
A sample is only useful if collecting it does not injure someone. Preventive safety means noticing and controlling hazards before work. Emergency response means acting in an organized way if something still goes wrong. This step develops prevention and preparation; the next two steps teach responses to injuries, heat illness, spills and evacuation.

Imagine that a partner becomes dizzy and confused in a remote field, or that a container of fertilizer is knocked over. Who knows where you are? How can you raise the alarm? Where can you move safely? These questions show why preparation matters. They are not an invitation to treat a casualty or clean a spill beyond your training.

Explain the purpose of today's work in your own words. If you have seen an emergency, you can reflect on what people did well or missed. You can equally use an invented example; sharing a personal experience is optional.

scenes.title: 1. Look around — and consider what you cannot see
scenes.lead: Before leaving the preparation area, listen to the trainer's short safety briefing. The trainer selects a safe, accessible site and confirms where sampling is permitted. Walk the route and identify uneven ground, holes, animal burrows and obstacles. Sprinkler heads at a field edge can be easy to miss and can cause a trip or damage to irrigation equipment.
scenes.narration:
Before leaving the preparation area, listen to the trainer's short safety briefing. The trainer selects a safe, accessible site and confirms where sampling is permitted. Walk the route and identify uneven ground, holes, animal burrows and obstacles. Sprinkler heads at a field edge can be easy to miss and can cause a trip or damage to irrigation equipment.

Check nearby machinery, reversing alarms and overhead electrical lines. Looking down at a phone while a tractor is moving removes the attention you need to stay clear. Stay outside the working area and use the agreed safe route; do not assume that the driver has seen you.

Irrigation pipes, gas pipes and electrical cables may also be buried. An apparently clear surface does not establish that digging is safe. Do not insert a probe, auger or spade until the trainer has confirmed clearance for that location. If a marking is missing or the situation is uncertain, stop and ask. A training diagram cannot locate real utilities.

scenes.title: 2. Make sure help can find you
scenes.lead: Tell the supervisor where the team is going and when it expects to return. Work with a partner in remote areas and agree how to stay in contact. Carry a charged phone or the communication device specified for the site, with the relevant emergency contacts available.
scenes.narration:
Tell the supervisor where the team is going and when it expects to return. Work with a partner in remote areas and agree how to stay in contact. Carry a charged phone or the communication device specified for the site, with the relevant emergency contacts available.

A phone does not replace the buddy system. Reception can fail, a battery can run out and an injured person may be unable to make a call. Before work, agree what to do if communication fails or someone does not return. Know the access route and meeting point so you can give useful directions to help.

scenes.title: 3. Know your equipment and your limits
scenes.lead: Do not operate machinery just because its controls look simple. Training, permission and an appropriate supervised setting come first. Check hand tools before use: the handle must be secure, the working part sound and clean, and defects reported. Do not use a damaged tool.
scenes.narration:
Do not operate machinery just because its controls look simple. Training, permission and an appropriate supervised setting come first. Check hand tools before use: the handle must be secure, the working part sound and clean, and defects reported. Do not use a damaged tool.

Carry sharp tools so the blade or point is directed down and away from people, with enough space around you. Follow the trainer's demonstration for the particular tool; do not swing it, balance it across a shoulder near others or leave it in a walkway. Clean tools and appropriate clean gloves also help avoid contaminating the soil sample.

Before handling a fertilizer, pesticide, soil amendment or test reagent, read its label and the current Safety Data Sheet, or SDS. Older documents may say MSDS. Find its hazards, handling and storage instructions, protective measures and emergency information. Do not guess a chemical's hazards from its container colour or a test-result chart.

scenes.title: 4. Plan for living things and weather
scenes.lead: Watch for snakes, stinging insects and harmful plants without approaching or disturbing them. Report a hazard and use the safe route agreed with the trainer. Biological hazards are not always obvious from a distance.
scenes.narration:
Watch for snakes, stinging insects and harmful plants without approaching or disturbing them. Report a hazard and use the safe route agreed with the trainer. Biological hazards are not always obvious from a distance.

Consider heat, sun and changing weather. Plan drinking water, suitable clothing, shade and rest breaks. Tell the trainer if conditions or your health change. A hat and water do not make it safe to ignore dizziness or confusion. Detailed heat-illness action is taught in the next step; here the priority is prevention and prompt reporting.

scenes.title: Choose protection for the hazard — not by habit
scenes.lead: Personal Protective Equipment, or PPE, is equipment worn to reduce exposure to a hazard. It supports a safe method; it does not make an unsafe site or unauthorized task acceptable. The right combination depends on the job, the material and the conditions.
scenes.narration:
Personal Protective Equipment, or PPE, is equipment worn to reduce exposure to a hazard. It supports a safe method; it does not make an unsafe site or unauthorized task acceptable. The right combination depends on the job, the material and the conditions.

Sturdy work boots provide grip and foot protection. Where impact or crushing hazards exist, the trainer specifies suitable protective toe caps, such as steel-toed boots. Long sleeves and trousers can reduce scratches, sun exposure and insect contact; a wide-brimmed hat helps against the sun. Clothing must also suit heat and the work being done.

Use eye protection selected for the hazard. Safety glasses used for particles are not automatically a substitute for chemical splash goggles. Gloves suitable for general soil work protect hands and can reduce sample contamination, but they are not necessarily suitable for a chemical.

scenes.title: Chemical protection needs a compatibility check
scenes.lead: For a chemical task, the glove material must be compatible with the actual chemical and exposure. Nitrile and neoprene are examples of materials, not a guarantee of protection against every product. Check the SDS and glove manufacturer's information with the trainer. Cotton or leather gloves can absorb liquid and hold it against the skin.
scenes.narration:
For a chemical task, the glove material must be compatible with the actual chemical and exposure. Nitrile and neoprene are examples of materials, not a guarantee of protection against every product. Check the SDS and glove manufacturer's information with the trainer. Cotton or leather gloves can absorb liquid and hold it against the skin.

Compare an unused fabric gardening glove with a compatible chemical-resistant glove, using clean props only. Explain why appearance and thickness alone cannot establish chemical resistance. Check that the selected equipment is intact and suitable before putting it on.

Depending on the risk assessment, chemical-resistant coveralls or an apron may also be required. Where harmful dust, vapour or mist may be inhaled, a respirator must be selected for the contaminant and task, with the appropriate filter or cartridge and training. Tight-fitting respiratory protection requires a suitable fit test. A picture of a mask, or a dust mask used for the wrong hazard, does not prove protection.

High-visibility clothing helps other workers see you near machinery, but it does not replace separation from moving equipment. Hearing protection, such as suitable earmuffs or earplugs, may be needed near loud engines or machinery. Use the protection and working arrangements specified for the actual site.

scenes.title: Bring the checks together before starting
scenes.lead: Build a five-point checklist rather than a list of equipment names. First: the site and route are safe, with permission and utility clearance. Second: tools are sound, clean and carried safely. Third: protection matches the task and any chemical information. Fourth: the supervisor knows the location and return time, and the buddy and communication arrangements are clear. Fifth: emergency contacts, access, meeting point, water and weather precautions are known.
scenes.narration:
Build a five-point checklist rather than a list of equipment names. First: the site and route are safe, with permission and utility clearance. Second: tools are sound, clean and carried safely. Third: protection matches the task and any chemical information. Fourth: the supervisor knows the location and return time, and the buddy and communication arrangements are clear. Fifth: emergency contacts, access, meeting point, water and weather precautions are known.

For each point, state what would make you stop. Examples include uncertain buried services, a loose tool handle, missing chemical information, a failed communication plan or a moving machine blocking the route. Report the problem and wait for a safe arrangement; ticking a box does not resolve a hazard.

Preparation, awareness and limits reduce the chance of making a bad situation worse. Completing this step does not qualify you as a first aider or certify your physical performance. Your trainer observes the practical task separately.

scenes.title: A shortcut beside the tractor
scenes.lead: A sampling team sees a sprinkler head and a hole on the shortest route. A tractor is reversing nearby. One partner says, “We have boots and a phone — let's go.”
scenes.narration:
A sampling team sees a sprinkler head and a hole on the shortest route. A tractor is reversing nearby. One partner says, “We have boots and a phone — let's go.”

Boots reduce some injury risks, but do not remove the hole, sprinkler or moving machine.

The team stays out of the machine's operating area, reports the route hazards and waits for a safe route agreed with the trainer.

They confirm the sampling location, utility clearance, expected return and contact arrangements before carrying the tools down and away from people.

Control the route and the work first. Equipment alone is not permission to proceed.

scenes.title: Two pairs of gloves on the bench
scenes.lead: The task involves a liquid reagent. There are fabric gloves and nitrile gloves, but no current SDS or compatibility information has been supplied.
scenes.narration:
The task involves a liquid reagent. There are fabric gloves and nitrile gloves, but no current SDS or compatibility information has been supplied.

Fabric can absorb a spill and hold it against the hand.

Nitrile is a possible material, but its name alone does not prove compatibility with this reagent.

Stop chemical handling and obtain the SDS, glove compatibility information and trainer's instructions. Select eye and other protection as well.

The correct action can be to stop for missing information, not choose the most convincing-looking item.
